figures.title: Putting on and taking off PPE
figures.caption: Take off the most contaminated item first and touch only the clean parts: the inside, the ties, the headband. Hand hygiene comes before putting anything on and right after taking everything off. The CDC also allows peeling the gown and gloves off together.
rows: 1st
Hand hygiene
Gloves, the dirtiest item
2nd
Gown, tied at the neck and waist
Goggles or face shield, by the headband
3rd
Mask, or an N95 respirator with a seal check
Gown, rolled inside out and away from the body
4th
Goggles or face shield
Mask or respirator, by the ties; an N95 comes off after leaving the room
5th
Gloves, pulled over the gown cuffs
Hand hygiene right away

figures.caption: Standard precautions apply to everyone; these are added on top. C. diff spores survive alcohol rub, so wash with soap and water after that room.
rows: Spreads by
Tiny particles that hang in the air
Large droplets within about 6 feet
Touching the client or surfaces
Examples
TB, measles, chickenpox, disseminated zoster
Influenza, pertussis, mumps, bacterial meningitis
MRSA, VRE, C. diff, scabies, RSV
Room
Private negative-pressure room, door closed
Private room, or 3 feet from others
Private room, or cohort with the same organism
Nurse wears
Fit-tested N95 respirator
Surgical mask
Gown and gloves

Client wears a surgical mask
Client wears a surgical mask
Cover the infected area

figures.title: Who comes first: priority rules
figures.caption: Rank clients by how fast harm comes if the nurse waits. Work down the rules and stop at the first one that separates them. In cardiac arrest the order becomes compressions, airway, breathing.

steps.title: Airway
steps.detail: Stridor, throat tightness, a swollen tongue or lips, gurgling secretions, or a lost gag reflex. Nothing else comes before it.

steps.title: Breathing
steps.detail: New shortness of breath, a rising respiratory rate, oxygen saturation falling below the client's usual level, a quiet chest in asthma.

steps.title: Circulation
steps.detail: Active bleeding, a falling blood pressure with a rising heart rate, new chest pain, a cold or pulseless limb.

steps.title: Other physical needs, then safety
steps.detail: Maslow: physiological needs (urinary retention, severe pain, a low glucose) come before safety, then love and belonging, then esteem.

steps.title: Acute and unstable before chronic and stable
steps.detail: A sudden change, like new confusion or new weakness, outranks a long-standing finding at the client's baseline, like 89% saturation in COPD.

steps.title: Unexpected before expected
steps.detail: A finding the condition or treatment doesn't explain comes first. Incisional pain after surgery or bruising at an injection site can wait.

steps.title: Actual before potential
steps.detail: A problem happening now outranks a risk, unless the risk is about to threaten life, like tingling after thyroid surgery that signals low calcium.

steps.title: Teaching and discharge last
steps.detail: Routine care, teaching and discharge paperwork come after every client is safe.

figures.title: Who does what: RN, LPN/LVN, assistive staff
figures.caption: The RN delegates tasks, never judgment, and stays accountable. Five rights: the right task, circumstance, person, directions and communication, and supervision and evaluation. Exact scope varies by state practice act and facility policy.
rows: RN
Assess, plan, teach and evaluate; care for unstable and newly admitted clients
Delegate assessment, teaching, evaluation or judgment
LPN/LVN
Stable, predictable clients; collect data; give oral, IM, subcut meds; reinforce teaching
Initial assessment, care planning, initial teaching, unstable clients
Assistive personnel
Hygiene, feeding, walking, turning, vital signs on stable clients, intake and output
Assess, teach, give medications, do sterile procedures, or judge what a finding means
Gray zones
IV therapy by an LPN/LVN, glucose checks by assistive staff
Allowed only as the state practice act and facility policy permit

figures.title: Mass casualty triage tags (START)
figures.caption: START sorts each adult in under a minute. Anyone who can walk is green. A client who isn't breathing gets the airway repositioned once: still apneic is black, breathing is red. Everyone else is red or yellow by breathing, perfusion and mental status.
rows: Red: immediate
Breathes over 30 a minute, no radial pulse or refill over 2 sec, or can't obey commands
Tension pneumothorax, hemorrhagic shock, airway burns
Yellow: delayed
Can't walk, but breathing, perfusion and mental status are adequate
Open fracture with good pulses, stable abdominal wound
Green: minor
Walks to the collection area when told
Sprains, small cuts, minor burns, closed fractures of a hand or arm
Black: expectant
Not breathing after the airway is repositioned, or injuries not survivable here
Massive open head injury, full-thickness burns over most of the body

figures.title: Using restraints safely
figures.caption: A restraint is a last resort for safety, never a punishment or a convenience. Monitoring and release intervals and order renewal limits are set by facility policy and regulation; follow the policy where you work.

steps.title: Try less restrictive measures first
steps.detail: Reorient, add a sitter or a bed alarm, lower the bed, hide or pad lines and tubes, involve family. Document what was tried.

steps.title: Get a provider order, never as needed
steps.detail: Time-limited, with the reason and the type of restraint. In an emergency, apply it and get the order right away. Renew it as policy requires.

steps.title: Apply the least restrictive device
steps.detail: Explain to the client and family. Pad bony areas, leave room for two fingers under the strap, keep the limb in normal alignment.

steps.title: Tie it to the bed frame, quick-release knot
steps.detail: Never to the side rail, which moves and can injure the client. The knot must come undone in seconds in an emergency.

steps.title: Check the client often
steps.detail: Circulation, sensation, skin, breathing, comfort and mental status, as often as policy requires (commonly every 15 to 30 minutes).

steps.title: Release and meet needs
steps.detail: Remove one restraint at a time, at least every 2 hours or per policy, for range of motion, skin care, toileting, fluids and food.

steps.title: Remove it as soon as it's safe
steps.detail: Stop once the behavior resolves; don't wait for the order to expire. Reapplying needs a new order. Document every check.

figures.title: Fire response: RACE, then PASS
figures.caption: Rescue anyone in immediate danger first. When a whole unit must leave, move walking clients first, then those in wheelchairs, then those confined to bed, going horizontally past fire doors before going down stairs. Never use an elevator.

steps.title: R: Rescue
steps.detail: Move clients in immediate danger away from the fire, starting with the room that is burning.

steps.title: A: Alarm
steps.detail: Pull the nearest fire alarm and call the facility's emergency number with the exact location.

steps.title: C: Contain
steps.detail: Close doors and windows to slow smoke and flames. Oxygen feeds a fire; it is shut off to the area as policy directs.

steps.title: E: Extinguish or evacuate
steps.detail: Fight only a small fire with a clear exit behind you. Otherwise leave and evacuate.

steps.title: P: Pull the pin
steps.detail: Hold the extinguisher upright and pull the pin to break the seal.

steps.title: A: Aim low
steps.detail: Point the nozzle at the base of the fire, not at the flames.

steps.title: S: Squeeze the handle
steps.detail: Squeeze slowly and evenly to release the extinguishing agent.

steps.title: S: Sweep side to side
steps.detail: Sweep across the base until the fire is out, and watch for it to flare up again.

figures.title: Informed consent: valid or not
figures.caption: The provider explains the procedure and obtains consent; the nurse witnesses the signature. If the client has doubts or questions, the nurse stops and calls the provider back before anything is signed.
rows: Explanation
From the provider: the procedure, risks, benefits, alternatives, right to refuse
Only the nurse explained it, or the client can't say what will be done
Nurse's signature
Witnesses that the client signed willingly and seems competent
Witnessing while the client says they don't understand
Mental state
Alert and able to weigh the choice
After an opioid or sedative, confused, intoxicated, or pressured
Language
A trained medical interpreter, noted on the form
A family member or child interpreting
Who signs
Competent adult; for a minor, a parent or guardian unless state law says otherwise
A relative signing for a competent adult
Emergency
Life-saving care when the client can't consent and no surrogate can be reached in time
Care that can safely wait, or care the client has already refused

figures.title: Therapeutic communication
figures.caption: Keep the focus on the client's feelings and let the client lead. The wrong answers usually reassure falsely, give advice, ask why, change the subject, or argue.
rows: Opening up
Open-ended: "Tell me more about that."
Closed or why questions: "Why did you do that?"
Feelings
Reflecting: "You sound frightened."
Minimizing: "Everyone feels that way."
Comfort
Offering self: "I'll sit with you for a while."
False reassurance: "Don't worry, it will be fine."
Decisions
Exploring: "What options have you thought about?"
Advice: "If I were you, I would..."
Meaning
Clarifying: "What do you mean by that?"
Judging: "That's a bad idea."
Voices and delusions
Presenting reality: "I don't hear voices, but you seem scared."
Arguing with the belief, or playing along with it
Pauses
Silence and active listening
Changing the subject or talking about yourself

figures.title: Responding to suicide risk
figures.caption: Take every hint seriously and ask about it directly. Risk rises with a specific plan, a lethal method at hand, prior attempts, and a sudden lift in mood or energy.

terms: (better off|easier)( if I( just)? (were|was|weren't|wasn't)| without me| dead)

steps.title: Ask directly
steps.detail: "Are you thinking of killing yourself?" Asking plainly does not plant the idea; it shows the topic is safe to talk about.

steps.title: Assess plan, means and timing
steps.detail: A specific plan, a lethal method within reach and a chosen time mean high risk. Ask about past attempts, hopelessness and substance use.

steps.title: Keep the client safe right now
steps.detail: High risk: never leave the client alone. Start one-to-one observation within sight or arm's reach, per the order and policy.

steps.title: Remove the means
steps.detail: Search belongings per policy; remove sharps, belts, cords, shoelaces, plastic bags and glass. Check that swallowed pills aren't being saved.

steps.title: Watch when mood suddenly lifts
steps.detail: Energy returns before mood in the first weeks of antidepressants. Sudden calm or giving things away can mean a decision has been made.

steps.title: Build a safety plan
steps.detail: Warning signs, coping steps, people and places to reach, the 988 crisis line, and removing firearms and saved medicines from the home.

steps.title: Report and document
steps.detail: Tell the provider and team, and record the client's own words, the risk level and the precautions in place.

figures.title: Antipsychotic side effects
figures.caption: Older drugs such as haloperidol and fluphenazine cause more movement effects; newer ones such as olanzapine and clozapine cause more weight gain and high glucose. Metoclopramide can cause the same movement effects.

terms: oculogyric( crisis)?|torticollis|(twisting|spasms?) of the neck|upward deviation of the eyes

rows: Acute dystonia
Hours to 5 days: painful spasm of the neck, jaw or tongue; eyes rolled upward
Urgent: IM or IV benztropine or diphenhydramine; protect the airway
Akathisia
Days to weeks: can't sit still, pacing, inner restlessness, often mistaken for anxiety
Report it; lower dose, propranolol or a benzodiazepine as ordered
Pseudo-parkinsonism
Weeks: shuffling gait, tremor, rigidity, mask-like face, drooling
Benztropine or another anticholinergic; dose change; fall precautions
Tardive dyskinesia
Months to years: lip smacking, tongue thrusting, chewing, writhing limbs
Screen with the AIMS scale; report early, as it may be permanent
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Any time, often early: high fever, lead-pipe rigidity, confusion, unstable BP
Emergency: stop the drug, cool, IV fluids, dantrolene or bromocriptine
Metabolic
Weight gain, high glucose and lipids, most with olanzapine and clozapine
Weight, waist, glucose and lipids at the start and on a schedule
Low white cells
Clozapine: fever, sore throat or mouth sores from agranulocytosis
Absolute neutrophil count before and during; report any sign of infection
Everyday effects
Dry mouth, constipation, urine retention, dizziness on standing, sunburn
Sugar-free gum, fluids and fiber, rise slowly, sunscreen

figures.title: Serotonin syndrome vs NMS
figures.caption: Both bring fever, a racing heart, swinging blood pressure and confusion; both are emergencies. Tell serotonin syndrome from neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) by the drug, the speed of onset, and the muscles: twitching versus rigid.
rows: Cause
An SSRI, SNRI or MAOI plus tramadol, a triptan, linezolid or St. John's wort
Any antipsychotic, most often a high-potency one or a fast dose increase
Onset
Fast: within hours of a new drug or higher dose
Slower: over 1 to 3 days, often in the first weeks
Muscles
Tremor, twitching, clonus, brisk reflexes
Severe lead-pipe rigidity, slow movement
Other signs
Agitation, sweating, dilated pupils, diarrhea; fever when severe
Very high fever, stupor, sweating, high creatine kinase (CK)
Treatment
Stop the drug; cooling, benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine
Stop the antipsychotic; cooling, IV fluids, dantrolene or bromocriptine
Course
Usually settles within 24 hours of stopping
Takes 1 to 2 weeks to resolve; muscle breakdown can cause kidney failure

figures.title: Alcohol withdrawal: what comes when
figures.caption: Count from the last drink. Tremor, seizures and hallucinosis come early; delirium tremens comes late, around day 2 to 4, and can kill. Benzodiazepines are dosed by the CIWA-Ar score, and thiamine goes in before glucose.

series.label: Tremor, anxiety, sweating
series.note: Starts 6 to 12 hours after the last drink, with nausea, a fast pulse and insomnia. Peaks around 24 to 36 hours.

series.label: Seizures
series.note: 6 to 48 hours, most often around 24 hours. Usually generalized tonic-clonic. Seizure precautions and benzodiazepines.

series.label: Hallucinosis
series.note: 12 to 48 hours. Mostly visual hallucinations while the client stays oriented, with fairly normal vital signs.

series.label: Delirium tremens
series.note: 48 to 96 hours: confusion, agitation, fever, fast pulse, high BP, drenching sweats. Lasts days; a medical emergency.

figures.title: Levels of anxiety
figures.caption: As anxiety rises, the client's attention narrows until they can't take in words at all. Teach only at mild or moderate levels; at severe and panic levels, stay with the client, keep sentences short and lower stimulation.

terms: impending doom|something terrible is happening|(I am|I'm) going to die|feeling of dying

rows: Mild
Alert and attentive; learns and solves problems well
A good time to teach
Moderate
Narrowed focus but can follow directions; faster pulse, pacing, trembling voice
Help the client focus; clear, simple directions; explore the feeling
Severe
Fixes on details, can't solve problems; headache, nausea, rapid breathing
Stay with the client; calm, quiet space; short sentences; no teaching
Panic
Terror, disorganized thinking, can't communicate or follow directions
Safety first: stay, few words, low stimulation, medication as ordered

figures.title: During and after a seizure
figures.caption: Protect the client; never restrain or put anything in the mouth. For a client at risk, keep the bed low, side rails padded per policy, oxygen and suction ready at the bedside, and IV access in place.

steps.title: Stay, call for help, note the time
steps.detail: Timing the seizure tells you when it has become an emergency.

steps.title: Protect from injury
steps.detail: Ease the client to the floor if upright, move furniture away, cushion the head, and loosen clothing at the neck.

steps.title: Nothing in the mouth, no restraint
steps.detail: Don't force in a tongue blade, fingers or an airway, and don't hold the limbs down.

steps.title: Turn to the side as soon as possible
steps.detail: Lets saliva drain and keeps the tongue from blocking the airway. Suction and oxygen as needed.

steps.title: Watch and describe
steps.detail: Where it started, the body parts involved, eye deviation, incontinence, and how long it lasted.

steps.title: Over 5 minutes: status epilepticus
steps.detail: Or seizures back to back without waking. Call the rapid response team; a benzodiazepine such as IV lorazepam per protocol.

steps.title: Afterward, let the client recover
steps.detail: Side-lying, airway and vital signs checked, injuries looked for, reoriented. Confusion and sleepiness afterward are expected.

figures.title: Preventing and responding to falls
figures.caption: Most falls happen when a client gets up alone, often to reach the bathroom. Screen everyone, then match the precautions to the risk. After a fall, assess before moving the client.

steps.title: Screen on admission and after changes
steps.detail: Use a tool such as the Morse Fall Scale. Reassess after a fall, surgery, a transfer, or new sedating medications.

steps.title: Know the big risk factors
steps.detail: A prior fall, confusion, unsteady gait, urgency or frequent toileting, dizziness on standing, and sedatives, opioids or diuretics.

steps.title: Make the room safe
steps.detail: Bed low and locked, call light and belongings within reach, a night light, a clear path, nonskid footwear.

steps.title: Round and toilet on a schedule
steps.detail: Check pain, position and toileting needs hourly; offer the bathroom before the client decides to go alone.

steps.title: Get up safely
steps.detail: Dangle at the bedside before standing and use a gait belt and the client's walker or cane. If the client starts to fall, ease them to the floor.

steps.title: Alarms and sitters, not restraints
steps.detail: Bed or chair alarms, a room near the station, a sitter. All four side rails up counts as a restraint and raises injury risk.

steps.title: After a fall, assess before moving
steps.detail: Stay and call for help; check breathing, injuries, a head strike, neuro status and vital signs. Notify the provider; file an incident report.

figures.title: Psychosis: symptoms and responses
figures.caption: Positive symptoms add something to normal experience; negative symptoms take something away and are often harder to treat. Never argue with a hallucination or delusion, and never play along with it.
rows: Hallucinations
Hears, sees or feels what isn't there; glances around, talks or listens to no one
Say you don't hear it but see the fear; focus on real, concrete activities
Command hallucinations
Voices order the client to harm self or others
Ask what the voices say and if the client can resist; keep everyone safe
Delusions
Fixed false beliefs: being poisoned, watched, controlled or specially chosen
Don't argue or agree; respond to the feeling; sealed foods if poison is feared
Disorganized speech
Loose associations, word salad, rhyming clang associations, made-up words
Say when you don't understand; use short, clear sentences
Negative symptoms
Flat affect, little speech, no drive or pleasure, withdrawal, poor hygiene
Short, frequent contacts; simple structured tasks; help with self-care
Catatonia
Motionless or rigid, limbs stay where placed, not eating or drinking
Meet fluid, food, skin and elimination needs; watch for sudden agitation

figures.title: Recognizing and reporting abuse
figures.caption: Nurses must report suspected child abuse, and in most states elder and dependent-adult abuse; a good-faith report needs no proof. Chart exactly what you see and the client's own words, without conclusions.
rows: Child
Injury that doesn't fit the story or the child's age, spiral fractures, patterned burns
Report to child protective services; proof isn't needed. Talk with the child alone
Older or dependent adult
Unexplained bruises, poor hygiene, pressure injuries, weight loss, missing money
Report as state law requires, usually to adult protective services; keep the client safe
Intimate partner
Injuries to the face, neck or arms, delayed care, a partner who won't leave the room
Screen alone; offer a safety plan and a hotline. Adult reporting laws vary by state
Sexual assault
Client discloses an assault; shock, numbness or fear
Preserve evidence: no bathing or changing first; forensic exam only with consent

figures.title: Advance directives and DNR orders
figures.caption: Facilities must ask every adult on admission whether they have an advance directive. A client who can still decide speaks for themselves; the document or the agent speaks only when the client cannot.
rows: Living will
States which life-sustaining treatments the client wants or refuses if unable to decide
Ask about it on admission and get a copy into the chart
Health care power of attorney
Names an agent to make decisions only when the client can't
While the client can decide, the agent can't override the client
DNR order
A provider's order: no CPR if breathing or the heart stops
All other care continues: comfort, medications, fluids, relieving choking
POLST form
Portable provider orders on current treatment limits for serious illness
Travels with the client; honor it in every care setting
Stopping treatment
A client who can decide may refuse or stop any treatment, even dialysis or a ventilator
Confirm the client is informed, support the choice, bring in palliative care
